commands.desc: List Mailcow container states as JSON
commands.tooltip: ps --format json prints one record per service with state and health, easy to feed into jq or monitoring scripts. Health shows how the Mailcow watchdog sees each container. Use plain ps for the human-readable table.

commands.desc: Show running processes inside Mailcow containers
commands.tooltip: top prints the live process list for every running container, mirroring the host ps output. Useful to confirm daemons like master (Postfix) or dovecot are actually running inside their containers. Process names here are container-internal, not host PIDs.

commands.desc: Validate the Mailcow compose file
commands.tooltip: config resolves and validates docker-compose.yml, failing with an error if it is malformed or references missing values. --quiet suppresses the resolved output and only reports problems. Run it after hand-editing the compose file or environment overrides.

commands.desc: List container images used by the Mailcow stack
commands.tooltip: images shows the repository, tag, and image ID behind each running service. Handy for checking which Mailcow release tag is deployed and whether services run consistent versions. Contrast with docker compose ps, which reports container state, not images.

commands.desc: Start Mailcow and remove orphan containers
commands.tooltip: up -d creates or starts every service defined in the compose file. --remove-orphans deletes containers not defined in the current file, cleaning up leftovers from renamed or removed services. Combined with a fresh git pull this is the standard Mailcow update startup step.

commands.desc: Pull the Postfix container image
commands.tooltip: pull fetches the latest image for a single service without touching running containers, here the mailcow/postfix image that hosts the MTA. Do this before up -d to stage an update. Omit the service name to pull every image.

commands.desc: Stop Mailcow and delete all its volumes
commands.tooltip: down --volumes stops every container and then removes the named volumes holding maildirs, the MySQL database, and Redis state. This permanently destroys all mail and configuration and is only appropriate for a full teardown. Use plain down to stop without losing data.

commands.desc: Restart every Mailcow service
commands.tooltip: restart stops and starts all services in dependency order in one step. Prefer it over down/up when a config change touched several containers, since it preserves volumes and container identity. Watch the watchdog container logs afterwards if a service fails to come back.

commands.desc: Restart the Rspamd spam filter container
commands.tooltip: restarting rspamd-mailcow reloads its scoring engine, fuzzy storage, and settings without touching mail delivery. Do this after pushing custom rspamd config files into data/conf/rspamd. In-flight scanning is brief, but queued mail is not lost.

commands.desc: Restart the Dovecot IMAP and POP3 container
commands.tooltip: dovecot-mailcow handles IMAP, POP3, and Sieve filtering for mailboxes. Restarting it drops existing client connections, so schedule it off-peak. Prefer this over killing the process, which can leave mailbox index locks behind.

commands.desc: Restart the Mailcow web frontend container
commands.tooltip: nginx-mailcow terminates HTTPS for the admin UI, SOGo webmail, and autodiscover endpoints. A restart reloads server blocks and certificates after changes to data/conf/nginx. Existing web sessions are re-established transparently.

commands.desc: Restart the Mailcow watchdog container
commands.tooltip: watchdog-mailcow monitors every service health and restarts unhealthy containers automatically. Restarting it resets its own state and can help when it loops restarting a healthy service. Check its logs with docker compose logs watchdog-mailcow first.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 Postfix container log lines
commands.tooltip: postfix-mailcow logs contain SMTP transactions, delivery attempts, and deferral reasons. --tail=100 keeps the output to the newest 100 lines so the noise stays manageable. Add -f to follow the log live while reproducing a problem.

commands.desc: Follow Dovecot logs with a 50 line backlog
commands.tooltip: This tails Dovecot auth, IMAP, and Sieve log lines in real time. Combined with --tail=50 you see context before the newest entries. Watch for repeated LOGIN failures, which point at brute-force attempts or broken clients.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 Rspamd log lines
commands.tooltip: Rspamd logs each scanned message with its score and matched rules, plus errors from the fuzzy and neural modules. Grep the output for rule names like BAYES_IS_SPAM to trace why a message scored as it did. Verbose per-message detail lives in the history, not here.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 nginx access and error lines
commands.tooltip: nginx-mailcow logs cover every HTTP request to the admin UI, SOGo, and autodiscover. Error lines about upstream timeouts point at php-fpm or SOGo being slow. Access lines with many 401s hint at API key or login problems.

commands.desc: Show the last 50 ACME certificate renewal lines
commands.tooltip: acme-mailcow runs acme.sh and handles Let's Encrypt issuance and renewal for your mail domains. Log lines here show when certificates were issued, renewed, or failed with validation errors. Failures usually mean the HTTP-01 or DNS-01 challenge could not be answered.

commands.desc: Show the last 50 watchdog restart events
commands.tooltip: The watchdog restarts containers whose health checks fail and logs every action here. Repeated restarts of the same service signal a real fault, not a transient blip. Cross-reference with the target container's own logs to find the root cause.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 SOGo groupware log lines
commands.tooltip: SOGo is the webmail, calendar, and contacts suite bundled with Mailcow. Its logs cover ActiveSync syncs, Sieve rule application, and WebDAV traffic. Errors here often explain missing calendar invites or contacts not syncing to phones.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 ClamAV scan log lines
commands.tooltip: clamd-mailcow runs the ClamAV daemon that virus-scans attachments in the rspamd pipeline. Log lines record signature database updates and scan errors. A stalled signature update leaves clamd answering with errors, which rspamd logs as a clamav failure.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 MySQL container log lines
commands.tooltip: mysql-mailcow holds the mailcow database with mailboxes, aliases, domains, and quarantine state. Log lines cover InnoDB recovery and query errors, and MySQL 8 containers log slow queries when enabled. Disk-full errors here take down the whole UI and mail delivery.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 PHP-FPM log lines
commands.tooltip: php-fpm-mailcow executes the Mailcow web application and its cron jobs. Log lines surface PHP fatal errors and warnings that the UI silently swallows. Recent entries with stack traces are the first place to look after a UI feature breaks.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 unbound DNS resolver log lines
commands.tooltip: unbound-mailcow is the recursive DNS resolver Mailcow uses for DNS lookups, MX checks, and SPF/DKIM validation. Its logs show cache events and upstream failures. If mail is intermittently deferred with DNS errors, check here for timeouts to upstream resolvers.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 ofelia cron scheduler log lines
commands.tooltip: ofelia-mailcow is the container that runs scheduled jobs inside the stack, such as quarantine notification dispatches and SOGo maintenance. Log lines record when each scheduled job fired and whether it completed. Missing job entries mean ofelia itself is unhealthy.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 OLE file scanner log lines
commands.tooltip: olefy-mailcow strips and inspects OLE attachments (Office documents) before they reach the mail pipeline. Log lines show extracted objects handed to ClamAV and any scan timeouts. Suspicious Office attachments are quarantined based on what olefy extracts.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 Docker API proxy log lines
commands.tooltip: dockerapi-mailcow exposes a restricted Docker API used by the watchdog to restart unhealthy containers. Its logs record every restart request the watchdog issues. If containers restart without a visible reason, the requests will be logged here.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 firewall container log lines
commands.tooltip: netfilter-mailcow maintains the iptables rules that protect the mail services, including fail2ban-style ban rules. Its logs show banned IPs and firewall rule reloads. Repeated bans for one IP usually mean brute-force SMTP or IMAP attempts.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 memcached log lines
commands.tooltip: memcached-mailcow caches sessions and rate-limit state for the web application. Its logs report evictions and connection limits. Frequent eviction lines suggest the cache is undersized for your session count.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 TLS policy daemon log lines
commands.tooltip: postfix-tlspol-mailcow is Mailcow's per-recipient TLS policy daemon that enforces TLS for outbound mail to specific domains. Log lines show policy lookups and any lookups that failed. Failures here make Postfix fall back to its default smtp_tls_security_level.

commands.desc: Show the last 100 Redis log lines
commands.tooltip: redis-mailcow stores Rspamd statistics, rate-limit counters, and the quarantine notification timestamp. Its logs record persistence snapshots and key evictions. Losing Redis is safe but resets statistics and rate-limit history.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postfix check
commands.desc: Verify Postfix configuration inside the container
commands.tooltip: postfix check validates main.cf, master.cf, and queue directory permissions inside the Postfix container. Silent output with exit code zero means the configuration is sane. Run it before restarting postfix-mailcow after any manual map change.

commands.desc: Dump the Mailcow mail queue as JSON
commands.tooltip: postqueue -j prints every queued message with its ID, sender, recipients, and reason for deferral in machine-readable JSON. Pipe it through jq to find all messages stuck on one destination. This is the container equivalent of mailq with richer output.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postqueue -s example.com
commands.desc: Show queue statistics for one destination
commands.tooltip: postqueue -s prints a per-destination summary of queued messages, showing how many are stuck sending to example.com. Useful to confirm a delivery outage against a specific mail host. The destination is matched against the queue's active transport domain.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postsuper -d ALL
commands.desc: Delete every message from the Postfix queue
commands.tooltip: postsuper -d ALL purges the entire mail queue including messages waiting on retry timers. This permanently drops mail that has not been delivered yet, so export the queue first if any of it matters. Prefer deleting individual IDs with postsuper -d QID.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postsuper -r ALL
commands.desc: Requeue every message for immediate retry
commands.tooltip: postsuper -r ALL resets the arrival time of all queued messages so Postfix retries them on the next queue run. Useful after fixing an outage that caused mass deferrals. It does not delete anything, unlike postsuper -d ALL.

commands.desc: Show the raw source of one queued message
commands.tooltip: postcat -q prints the envelope and message content of a single queue file identified by its queue ID, exactly as stored. Grep it for headers and Received lines to trace where a stuck message came from. The queue ID comes from postqueue -p or postqueue -j.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postconf transport_maps
commands.desc: Show the transport map source Postfix uses
commands.tooltip: postconf transport_maps resolves the parameter and prints the actual map definition, which in Mailcow points at the SQL maps under /opt/postfix/conf/sql. Those SQL maps let Postfix query MySQL for transports instead of static files. Same trick works for virtual_alias_maps and virtual_mailbox_maps.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postmap -q user@example.com /opt/postfix/conf/sql/virtual_alias_maps.cf
commands.desc: Query a Mailcow SQL alias map directly
commands.tooltip: postmap -q looks up one key in a map file, here asking the virtual_alias_maps SQL map where mail to user@example.com is redirected. It runs the same SQL query Postfix would run, so it proves the map and database connection work. Use it before blaming aliases for a delivery problem.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec postfix-mailcow postfix flush
commands.desc: Flush all queued mail for immediate delivery
commands.tooltip: postfix flush tells the queue manager to attempt delivery of every deferred message right now instead of waiting for the next retry timer. Useful after fixing an outage, but do not run it repeatedly while a destination is still down. See postqueue -f for the unprivileged variant.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm expunge -u user@example.com mailbox Trash ALL
commands.desc: Permanently delete all mail in a mailbox folder
commands.tooltip: doveadm expunge removes messages matching the given search, here every message in Trash, and deletion is immediate and irreversible. Add a date filter such as BEFORE 01-Jan-2026 to keep recent mail. Test with doveadm search using the same criteria first.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm force-resync -u user@example.com INBOX
commands.desc: Rebuild the index for a corrupted mailbox
commands.tooltip: force-resync drops Dovecot's index and cache files for the given mailbox and rebuilds them from the maildir on disk. Use it when IMAP shows phantom messages, wrong counts, or messages that cannot be opened. The underlying mail is untouched.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm quota recalc -u user@example.com
commands.desc: Recalculate a mailbox quota usage
commands.tooltip: quota recalc recounts the bytes and messages a mailbox uses against its quota. Run it after moving or restoring maildirs, when the UI shows a quota that disagrees with reality. The Mailcow docs recommend it after any manual maildir manipulation.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm quota get -u user@example.com
commands.desc: Show quota usage and limits for one mailbox
commands.tooltip: quota get prints the current usage and configured limit for each quota root of the user. Mailcow enforces the per-mailbox quota set in the admin UI through these roots. Values are shown in bytes and as a percentage.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm who
commands.desc: List active IMAP and POP3 sessions
commands.tooltip: doveadm who shows currently connected clients with their username, protocol, and source IP. Handy for spotting a mailbox that is open from many IPs, a sign of a leaked password. Pair it with doveadm kick to disconnect suspicious sessions.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm kick '192.0.2.50'
commands.desc: Disconnect all sessions from one IP address
commands.tooltip: doveadm kick drops every IMAP or POP3 session originating from the given IP, forcing clients to reconnect. Standard move after seeing brute-force attempts or a compromised client on that address. The Mailcow netfilter firewall may ban the IP separately.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm reload
commands.desc: Reload Dovecot configuration without dropping sessions
commands.tooltip: doveadm reload signals Dovecot to re-read its configuration, applying changes while keeping existing connections alive. Use it after editing conf.d snippets that Dovecot owns. Structural changes still require a full container restart.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm search -u user@example.com mailbox INBOX subject 'invoice'
commands.desc: Find messages matching a search in a mailbox
commands.tooltip: doveadm search prints the UIDs of messages matching the given search, here unread subject lines in INBOX. It runs the same search engine as IMAP SEARCH. Follow up with doveadm fetch to read the raw message of a found UID.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm fetch -u user@example.com 'uid text' mailbox INBOX
commands.desc: Print the raw text of every INBOX message
commands.tooltip: doveadm fetch dumps the requested fields, here UID plus the full message text, for messages in the mailbox. Scope it down with a search, for example 'uid text' mailbox INBOX subject 'invoice', before running on a large mailbox. Output is raw RFC822 content.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm mailbox status -u user@example.com 'messages vsize' INBOX
commands.desc: Show message count and size for a mailbox
commands.tooltip: mailbox status reports the named fields for the given mailbox, here total messages and virtual size in bytes. Useful for a quick sanity check of what the UI should display. Field names come from the doveadm mailbox status documentation.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec dovecot-mailcow doveadm mailbox list -u user@example.com
commands.desc: List every mailbox folder of a user
commands.tooltip: mailbox list enumerates all folders the user has, including subscribed and hidden ones. Compare it with what the mail client shows to find subscriptions that drifted. Add the -s flag to list only subscribed folders.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec -u sogo sogo-mailcow sogo-tool backup -F ALL /etc/sogo user@example.org
commands.desc: Back up a SOGo user's calendar and contacts
commands.tooltip: sogo-tool backup exports a user's SOGo data, here everything from the default store into /etc/sogo. SOGo is the webmail and groupware suite behind Mailcow's calendar and contacts. Restore the resulting files with sogo-tool restore.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec -u sogo sogo-mailcow sogo-tool restore -F ALL /etc/sogo user@example.org
commands.desc: Restore a SOGo user's calendar and contacts
commands.tooltip: sogo-tool restore imports the backup files found in /etc/sogo for the given user, overwriting that user's current SOGo data. SOGo is the groupware suite providing calendars and contacts in Mailcow. Run the matching backup first and confirm the user is the right one, because the restore is destructive.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm dkim_keygen -d example.com -s default
commands.desc: Generate a DKIM key pair and print its DNS record
commands.tooltip: rspamadm dkim_keygen creates a DKIM signing key for the domain and prints the TXT record to publish in DNS. DKIM is the authentication scheme that lets receivers verify mail really came from your domain. Publish the printed record at default._domainkey.example.com.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm dkim_keygen -d example.com -s mailcow -b 2048 -k /etc/rspamd/dkim/mailcow.key
commands.desc: Generate a DKIM key with a custom selector and file
commands.tooltip: This variant writes the private key to /etc/rspamd/dkim/mailcow.key and prints only the public DNS record, which Mailcow's docs use for manual setups. The selector mailcow must match the TXT record name mailcow._domainkey.example.com. Keep the private key inside the container and readable by rspamd only.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamc -h rspamd:11333 symbols < /tmp/message.eml
commands.desc: Score a message file with the live Rspamd engine
commands.tooltip: rspamc sends the message on stdin to the Rspamd worker listening on rspamd:11333 and prints every rule hit with its score. This reproduces exactly how Mailcow would score that mail. Use it to test whether a message would land in quarantine before delivery.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamc -h rspamd:11333 learn_spam /tmp/spam.eml
commands.desc: Train Rspamd's Bayesian filter on a spam sample
commands.tooltip: learn_spam feeds the message into Rspamd's statistical classifier so future similar mail scores higher. Feed a few dozen clearly labeled samples for the filter to be effective. The learned state lives in Redis, so it survives rspamd restarts.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamc -h rspamd:11333 stat
commands.desc: Show Rspamd statistics summary
commands.tooltip: stat reports messages scanned, learned, and the current actions distribution from the Rspamd worker. A healthy filter shows a realistic share of reject and add-header actions. Numbers come from the running worker, not from log files.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamc -h rspamd:11333 counters
commands.desc: Show per-rule hit counters in Rspamd
commands.tooltip: counters prints how often each rule matched over the statistics window, revealing which rules dominate scoring. Rules firing on every message, such as missing headers, may deserve tuning. The counters reset when the statistics period expires.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm control reload
commands.desc: Reload Rspamd configuration live
commands.tooltip: rspamadm control reload makes Rspamd re-read its configuration files without dropping the worker. Use it after editing custom configs under data/conf/rspamd. Unlike a container restart it keeps statistics and learned data in memory.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm control stat
commands.desc: Query Rspamd control socket statistics
commands.tooltip: control stat reads the master statistics from the control socket, including scanned and learned message counts. It is the authoritative view of the whole Rspamd process, not one worker. Pair it with rspamc stat to compare worker-level numbers.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm configtest
commands.desc: Test Rspamd configuration syntax
commands.tooltip: configtest parses every Rspamd config file and reports syntax or logic errors with file and line references. Run it after hand-editing custom maps or modules. Silent success means the config is loadable.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec rspamd-mailcow rspamadm history
commands.desc: Browse recent scan results in Rspamd
commands.tooltip: rspamadm history opens an interactive browser over the last scanned messages stored in Redis, showing scores, rules, and per-message details. It is the CLI twin of the Mailcow UI history tab. Messages drop out after the configured history retention.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec redis-mailcow redis-cli DEL Q_LAST_NOTIFIED
commands.desc: Reset the quarantine notification timestamp in Redis
commands.tooltip: DEL Q_LAST_NOTIFIED removes the key that records when the last quarantine notification round was sent. Combined with resetting the notified flag in MySQL, this makes Mailcow resend quarantine digests. Run it only when you deliberately want to re-notify users.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec redis-mailcow redis-cli INFO memory
commands.desc: Show Redis memory usage
commands.tooltip: INFO memory reports used memory, peak usage, and fragmentation for the Redis instance that backs Rspamd statistics. A value near maxmemory forces evictions of stats and rate-limit state. Check the maxmemory setting if evictions appear.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec redis-mailcow redis-cli DBSIZE
commands.desc: Count keys stored in Redis
commands.tooltip: DBSIZE returns the number of keys in the default database, a quick health signal for the Redis instance. A sudden drop suggests Redis restarted and statistics were lost. Sudden growth can mean a runaway counter or queue.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec redis-mailcow redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory
commands.desc: Show the Redis maxmemory limit
commands.tooltip: CONFIG GET maxmemory prints the configured memory cap for the Redis instance. Mailcow sets a modest limit because Redis only holds statistics and counters. Raise it only if you see frequent eviction warnings in the redis logs.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec mysql-mailcow mysql -u mailcow -p mailcow -e 'UPDATE quarantine SET notified=0;'
commands.desc: Mark all quarantined messages as unnotified
commands.tooltip: This resets the notified flag on every quarantine row so the next notification round reports all of them. It is the MySQL half of Mailcow's documented quarantine re-notification procedure. It affects the whole table, so users will receive digests again.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec mysql-mailcow mysql -u mailcow -p mailcow -e 'SELECT COUNT(*) AS q FROM quarantine;'
commands.desc: Count quarantined messages in the database
commands.tooltip: This runs a direct SQL query against the mailcow database, here counting rows in the quarantine table. Useful to confirm the quarantine really is empty after a purge. The password in -p matches the one stored in mailcow.conf.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec mysql-mailcow mysql -u mailcow -p mailcow -e 'SELECT username, active FROM mailbox LIMIT 20;'
commands.desc: List mailboxes and their active flag from MySQL
commands.tooltip: This queries the mailbox table directly to see every mailbox and whether it is enabled. Faster than paging through the UI when auditing accounts. The active column controls whether login and delivery are permitted.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec mysql-mailcow mysqldump -u mailcow -p mailcow mailcow | gzip > /backup/mailcow-db.sql.gz
commands.desc: Dump the Mailcow database to a compressed file
commands.tooltip: mysqldump exports the whole mailcow schema and data, piped through gzip into a dated backup file. The dump contains mailboxes, aliases, domains, and quarantine state but not maildirs. Restore it with mysql < backup.sql if the database is ever lost.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec -T unbound-mailcow drill example.com MX @127.0.0.1
commands.desc: Resolve MX records through the Mailcow resolver
commands.tooltip: drill queries the unbound resolver listening inside the unbound-mailcow container, bypassing any local DNS config. unbound is the recursive resolver Mailcow uses for MX, SPF, and DKIM lookups. Use it to prove DNS answers are correct from Mailcow's own point of view.

commands.desc: Check whether the ClamAV daemon is responsive
commands.tooltip: clamdscan --ping sends a PING command to the clamd daemon and exits successfully when it answers. clamd is the virus scanner that checks attachments for the mail pipeline. A timeout here explains attachment errors and requires a clamd-mailcow restart.

commands.desc: Test the nginx configuration inside the container
commands.tooltip: nginx -t parses every server block and reports syntax errors with file and line numbers. Run it before restarting nginx-mailcow after editing files under data/conf/nginx. Exit code zero means the config is valid and safe to reload.

commands.cmd: docker compose -f /opt/mailcow-dockerized/docker-compose.yml exec nginx-mailcow nginx -s reload
commands.desc: Reload nginx config without dropping connections
commands.tooltip: nginx -s reload tells the running master process to re-read its configuration and apply changes gracefully. Existing connections finish, new connections use the new config. Do this after nginx -t passes instead of restarting the container.

commands.desc: Update Mailcow to the latest release
commands.tooltip: update.sh pulls the newest code and images, then brings the stack up with the new version. Run it from the Mailcow directory, usually with sudo, and keep the branch in mailcow.conf on a supported release. Back up first, because updates can change the database schema.

commands.desc: Generate or repair the Mailcow configuration
commands.tooltip: generate_config.sh creates mailcow.conf from your answers, or regenerates missing pieces when the file is corrupt. It walks through hostname, timezone, and mail settings interactively. Existing containers are not touched until you run update.sh or up -d afterwards.

commands.desc: Back up maildirs and prune backups older than a week
commands.tooltip: This runs the Mailcow backup script for the vmail target, which snapshots every user's maildir into the backup location configured in mailcow.conf. --delete-days 7 removes backups older than seven days. Schedule it nightly to keep mail recoverable.

commands.desc: Back up the Mailcow database and prune old copies
commands.tooltip: The mysql target dumps the mailcow database with mailboxes, aliases, and quarantine state into the configured backup directory. --delete-days 7 prunes backups older than a week. Pair it with the vmail target for a complete recovery set.

commands.desc: Back up Rspamd statistics and learned data
commands.tooltip: The rspamd target snapshots the Redis-backed statistics and Bayesian learning that tune spam filtering. Restoring it after a reinstall keeps your filter calibration intact. Without it, the filter starts untrained and spam accuracy drops.

commands.desc: Restore the Mailcow stack from a full backup
commands.tooltip: restore all unpacks the named backup file and writes maildirs, the database, and configuration back into the stack. It overwrites current data, so verify the file and the target host before running. Follow the script's prompts and restart the stack afterwards.

commands.desc: Reset the Mailcow administrator password
commands.tooltip: mailcow-reset-admin.sh regenerates the admin password and prints the new one, recovering access when the UI login is lost. It updates the password hash in the database directly. Run it with sudo from the Mailcow directory and change the password again in the UI.

commands.desc: Delete Mailcow TLS certificates so they regenerate
commands.tooltip: Removing the ssl directory forces Mailcow to recreate self-signed certificates on the next up, and lets acme-mailcow re-issue Let's Encrypt certificates. Mail and web services fail TLS handshakes until the stack restarts. Export any custom certificates first because they are gone for good.

commands.desc: Enable garbage collection for deleted maildirs
commands.tooltip: MAILDIR_GC_TIME sets how long, in minutes, a deleted mailbox's maildir survives before the garbage collector purges it from disk. Without it, maildirs of deleted mailboxes can linger indefinitely. Restart the stack after appending it so the setting is picked up.

commands.desc: List all mailboxes via the Mailcow API
commands.tooltip: The v1 API authenticates with the X-API-Key header, where the key comes from the admin UI under System, API. This call returns every mailbox with its quota, active flag, and attributes as JSON. Pipe through jq to filter on fields.

commands.desc: Show one mailbox's full details via the API
commands.tooltip: The mailbox address in the URL path selects a single mailbox and returns its complete attribute set. Faster than scanning the full mailbox list for one account. The address must be URL-encoded if it contains special characters.

commands.desc: Create a mailbox through the Mailcow API
commands.tooltip: This POST creates the mailbox jane@example.com with the given password and 10 GB quota in one call. The response includes the new mailbox's details or an error message. Set the domain's default values first so the mailbox inherits sensible limits.

commands.desc: Delete a mailbox and its maildir via the API
commands.tooltip: The items array names the mailboxes to remove, and deletion also schedules the user's maildir for garbage collection. This is permanent: mail is unrecoverable once the maildir is purged. Export the account with IMAP or backup the vmail target first.

commands.desc: Create an alias that forwards to a mailbox
commands.tooltip: This creates info@example.com as an alias whose mail is delivered to jane@example.com. The goto field can hold several comma-separated recipients. Aliases do not consume quota and cannot log in by themselves.

commands.desc: Delete one or more aliases via the API
commands.tooltip: The items array names the alias addresses to remove. Deleting an alias immediately stops delivery to its targets, so mail to that address bounces. Verify nothing important still uses the alias before removing it.

commands.desc: Add a mail domain through the Mailcow API
commands.tooltip: This registers example.com with limits for aliases, mailboxes, default per-mailbox quota, and total domain quota. MX and autodiscover DNS records must already point at your server. New mailboxes inherit defquota unless overridden.

commands.desc: List all domains via the Mailcow API
commands.tooltip: This returns every domain with its quota usage, alias and mailbox counts, and active state. Useful for audits of how many domains the server hosts. Filter with jq to find domains over their quota.

commands.desc: List messages held in quarantine via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns messages flagged as spam and held for review, with sender, recipient, subject, and reason. Quarantine is where Rspamd puts mail scored above the reject threshold. Release or delete individual items with edit/qitem and delete/qitem.

commands.desc: Release a quarantined message for delivery
commands.tooltip: The action release delivers the listed quarantine IDs to their original recipients, bypassing the spam hold. Useful when a legitimate message was caught. The ID comes from the quarantine listing and is tied to the stored message copy.

commands.desc: Release a message and train the filter as ham
commands.tooltip: The learnham action delivers the quarantined message and feeds it to Rspamd's Bayesian filter as legitimate mail. This both fixes the false positive and makes the filter less likely to catch similar mail. The learned state persists in Redis.

commands.desc: Delete quarantined messages permanently
commands.tooltip: The items array names quarantine entries whose stored message copies are deleted without delivery. This is irreversible, so review the sender and subject first. Use it to purge old spam instead of releasing it.

commands.desc: Generate a DKIM key pair for a domain
commands.tooltip: This creates a 2048-bit DKIM signing key for example.com under the selector default. DKIM lets receiving servers verify mail authenticity, so publish the returned TXT record at default._domainkey.example.com. Without the DNS record, signed mail fails verification.

commands.desc: Delete a DKIM key pair for a domain
commands.tooltip: Removing the DKIM key stops Mailcow from signing mail for the domain, and receivers that still verify the old record will fail DKIM checks. That typically worsens spam scores and deliverability. Export the private key first if you may need it again.

commands.desc: Show the DKIM DNS records for a domain
commands.tooltip: This returns the DNS record to publish for the domain's DKIM selector, including the public key. Compare it with what is actually published using dig to debug failing DKIM verification. The selector appears in the returned record name.

commands.desc: Add a BCC copy rule for a mailbox
commands.tooltip: This adds a blind-copy rule where every message sent by jane@example.com is also delivered to archive@example.com. BCC rules are the standard way Mailcow archives sent and received mail. The type field selects sender or recipient direction.

commands.desc: Show one BCC rule by its ID
commands.tooltip: This fetches a single BCC rule identified by its numeric ID, showing the local address, blind-copy destination, and direction. Use it to confirm a rule before editing or deleting it. The ID appears in the list returned by the BCC endpoints.

commands.desc: Delete BCC copy rules by ID
commands.tooltip: The items array holds the numeric IDs of BCC rules to remove, which stops the blind copies immediately. Archiving setups lose coverage the moment the rule is gone. Confirm the ID with get/bcc first.

commands.desc: List the Postfix queue via the Mailcow API
commands.tooltip: This returns every message currently in the Postfix queue with ID, sender, recipients, and deferral reason. Equivalent to postqueue -p but over HTTP with the same API key. Useful for scripts that alert on queue growth.

commands.desc: Delete queued messages without bounce notices
commands.tooltip: The super_delete action removes the listed queue IDs and suppresses bounce messages to the senders, unlike the plain delete action. Mail that is still undelivered is dropped permanently. Verify the IDs against get/mailq/all before deleting.

commands.desc: Toggle a mailbox attribute via the API
commands.tooltip: The attr field selects which mailbox property to change, here active, applied to every address in items. Setting active disables login and delivery while keeping the maildir intact. Other attrs such as password or quota follow the same pattern.

commands.desc: Set a per-mailbox sending rate limit
commands.tooltip: This limits jane@example.com to 50 messages per minute, the frame given by rl_frame. Rate limits are enforced by Postfix and Rspamd together to throttle compromised accounts. Use a larger frame such as hour for gentler limits.

commands.desc: Set a custom spam score threshold for a mailbox
commands.tooltip: This overrides the global spam score for the listed mailboxes, here making jane@example.com quarantine anything Rspamd scores above 5. Lower values catch more spam but raise false positives. The global threshold stays in the Rspamd config.

commands.desc: Set an email footer for a domain
commands.tooltip: This appends the given footer text to outgoing mail from the listed domains. Mailcow injects footers during delivery, so stored mail is unchanged. HTML footers are supported with the appropriate markup in the footer field.

commands.desc: Configure quarantine digest notifications
commands.tooltip: This enables the daily quarantine digest that tells users which of their mail is held. The interval accepts values like hourly, daily, or weekly. Users can still manage quarantined mail from the UI regardless of digest settings.

commands.desc: Fetch recent Dovecot logs via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the tail of the Dovecot log with auth and IMAP events as JSON. Quick way to scan for failed logins without shelling into the container. The same pattern works for other get/logs endpoints.

commands.desc: Fetch recent Postfix logs via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the tail of the Postfix log showing SMTP transactions and delivery results. Useful to confirm a message left the server or find the deferral reason. Combine with get/mailq/all for a full queue picture.

commands.desc: Fetch recent SMTP authentication logs via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the SASL authentication log, listing every successful and failed SMTP login. A burst of failures from one IP signals a brute-force attack on the submission port. Pair it with netfilter logs to confirm bans were applied.

commands.desc: Fetch Rspamd scan history via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the recent scan history with scores, actions, and matched rules for each message. The data mirrors the History tab in the admin UI. Use it to find why a specific message was classified as spam.

commands.desc: Fetch firewall ban logs via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns netfilter events showing which IPs were banned and why. Mailcow's netfilter container maintains the iptables rules that block abusive senders. Persistent bans for one IP usually mean repeated auth failures.

commands.desc: Fetch API access logs via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the audit trail of API requests, including which key called which endpoint. Review it to spot unexpected API activity that could mean a leaked key. Rotate the key in the admin UI if you see calls you do not recognize.

commands.desc: Check health of all Mailcow containers via API
commands.tooltip: This returns every container with its state and health as seen by the watchdog. A container stuck unhealthy shows up here before mail delivery breaks. Poll it in monitoring scripts instead of parsing docker ps.

commands.desc: Show vmail storage usage via the API
commands.tooltip: This reports the disk usage of the vmail volume that holds all maildirs, plus per-user totals where available. Watch it to plan disk upgrades before the mail store fills up. A full vmail volume stops delivery entirely.

commands.desc: Show the installed Mailcow version via the API
commands.tooltip: This returns the running Mailcow version, which helps confirm whether an update actually applied. Compare it with the latest release on GitHub before planning an upgrade. The version string matches what the UI shows in the bottom-left corner.
